source.title: Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages
source.authors: Xinpeng Wang; Mingyang Wang; Yihong Liu; Hinrich Schütze; Barbara Plank

record.tranche_reason: The study uses activation-based refusal-vector extraction and ablation/addition to investigate multilingual transfer. Its results concern cross-language refusal mechanisms, not the claim versions’ fine-tuning, aligned/base token-position KL, opening-token bypasses, parameter/rank localization, causes of shallowness, or deepening training.
record.gate_note: The paper reports multilingual harmful-prompt compliance before and after activation-vector interventions, and measures refusal-vector geometry and harmful/harmless representation clustering. These are related findings, but the interventions are not the fine-tuning, compliant-prefix, suffix, decoding, weight/rank, or training-objective tests named by the claim versions. The paper also reports harmful-prompt compliance rates for baseline models across languages.
record.test_reason: The study extracts difference-in-means refusal directions from activations and ablates or adds them across 14 languages. It does no harmful or benign fine-tuning (V1, V2) and no aligned-vs-base per-token KL by response position (V3); its first-token KL is only a filter for choosing vectors. It uses no prefill, suffix or decoding attack (V4). It localizes nothing in weights or ranks (V5), since activation-space directions are a different construct. It does not study causes of shallowness (V6) or deepening training (V7). It neither cites the original sources nor relies on their finding, so T6 fits better than the record's T4. Its findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Add that transfer holds only across safety-aligned languages: Yoruba-derived vectors transfer poorly, and Yoruba responds weakly to vector addition. The authors attribute cross-lingual jailbreaks to weak harmful/harmless separation, not to a missing refusal direction.
record.recipe_differences: No harmful/benign fine-tuning or token-position aligned/base KL analysis. The study uses difference-in-means activation vectors and residual-stream ablation/addition across languages.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by language alignment: Yoruba is less responsive to refusal-vector interventions than safety-aligned languages. The study also selects intervention locations using refusal-score reduction and a first-token KL filter.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a 'jailbreak vector' (bypassed minus refused harmful means) makes 20–100% of refused samples comply; subtracting it restores refusal in most bypassed samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A bypassed-vs-refused activation direction causally modulates harmful compliance across languages.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal vectors derived from Yoruba, a safety-misaligned language, transfer poorly to other languages, except partly in gemma-2-9B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-lingual transfer of refusal directions depends on the source language being safety-aligned.

record.problems: The study tests a selected set of 14 languages and notes results may not extend to languages with extremely limited pretraining data. Several cross-language intervention results are presented in figures without per-condition numerical values in the text. Compliance judgments for non-English outputs use back-translation and WildGuard. Table 1 and its prose disagree on Qwen2.5-7B Yoruba compliance (74.0% versus 74.9%).
record.rows_left_out: Did not extract the full language-by-model baseline compliance matrix in Table 1, all target-language-by-model cells in Figures 1–3 and 9, or every language-specific result in Appendix Tables 6–7; these exceed the compact coverage chosen for the related findings, and many are figure-only. Also omitted the Table 5 Silhouette Scores for additional languages because the principal Table 2 language comparisons are retained.

untested.parts: No aligned-vs-base per-position KL; first-token KL is used only to filter vectors.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attacks; the bypass is by activation ablation.
Activation directions only; no weight- or rank-level localization.
No analysis of the data or objective causing shallowness.

missing.what: Jailbreak-vector addition and subtraction compliance rates by model and language

record.verdict_notes: This is a multilingual refusal-direction study in the line of Arditi et al. Activation-direction ablation is not the opening-token bypass of V4, nor the parameter or rank localization of V5. Compliance was judged by WildGuard on back-translated outputs.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on benign or ordinary instruction data.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL comparison across response positions; first-token KL is used for ablation filtering, not this claim.
No compliant opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding-change tests.
Activation-space refusal vectors are ablated or added; the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety.
No test of how data or training objectives produce shallowness.
No training to deepen safety beyond initial tokens, or evaluation of whether such training holds up.
